newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors' appetite seen keeping pound firm.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors' appetite seen keeping pound firm.

text.p: Japanese brokerage houses are expected to keep boosting the British pound as they feed yield-hungry domestic retail investors with sterling-based bonds, underwriting sources and dealers said on Thursday.
"They (sterling-based bonds) are very popular. Some of them were absorbed by private investors in seconds," one senior underwriter at a major Japanese securities firm said.
Underwriting sources said many firms planned to boost their lineup of sterling-denominated bonds as demand proved strong after a series of offerings.
They estimated that brokerages had lead-managed a total of about 800 million pounds worth of sterling-based bonds since adding them to their menu late last year.
Meanwhile, currency dealers said active sterling buying by those brokers had become one of the key reasons behind the stellar rise of the pound against the yen this week.
The pound stood at around 203.60/70 yen by late Tokyo on Thursday. It broke through the crucial 200 yen barrier on Wednesday for the first time since October 1992.

"Basically, sterling is an attractive currency, especially after the Aussie lost attractiveness (following rounds of credit easing last year)," said Hiroshi Yoshino, foreign exchange division manager at Yamaichi Securities.
Many domestic securities firms are currently telling retail investors to shift their foreign bonds assets to high-yielding sterling from the Australian dollar.
More and more, Japanese investors are seeking higher returns on their holdings as domestic interest rates continue to crawl at low levels, dealers said.

Dual-currency bonds, particularly the yen/Australian dollar samurai, had been the main source of investment for retail investors. But most dual samurais are now issued in yen/U.S. dollars, after Australian interest rates eased last year.
"Retail interest is growing more in the dollar and sterling," said Mikio Sugihara, chief manager of global capital markets group at Nomura Securities.
In January, Nomura lead-managed 300 million pounds worth of 6.2 percent three-year Eurobonds issued by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) for the first time.
The EBRD bonds sold out, and Nomura expects to offer more such bonds in the future.
"The dollar is very familiar to private investors, while people look for high yields in sterling-based bonds," Sugihara said.

Besides Nomura, domestic brokerage houses such as Nikko Securities have lead-managed 100 million pounds worth of Eurobonds, also issued by the EBRD, and Yamaichi Securities has managed 250 million pounds worth of Eurobonds issued by the International Financial Corp.
Some analysts, however, said the pound could carry too many risks, as it typically moved wildly.

The pound was battered temporarily late last month when Toyota Motor Corp president Hiroshi Okuda warned that the carmaker would turn its attention to continental Europe if Britain stayed out of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Just look how the pound plunged after the Toyota president's comments...it's scary," one analyst said.
"Individual investors may not think about holding (sterling-based bonds) for too long," he added.
